texts.orig: 1 What You Are Building

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A small company wants a file drop that its own tools can talk to: list what is there, fetch a file, store a file, with a digest to prove the file arrived intact. A colleague has written the protocol down - the ETP/1 Specification - and your job is to build the server and the client from that document alone, the way real network software is built from RFCs. Then you prove it works, not by saying so, but by capturing it on the wire and explaining what the capture shows.

texts.orig: 4.1 Capture your own sessions
texts.text: 4.1 Capture your own sessions

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In your Lab 0 VM, from your repository root, using your own server and client. Pick a port (5000 below) and keep it throughout. Use a test file of random bytes between 200 and 400 KiB. Loopback carries segments of up to about 64 KB, so a file that size makes the GET response cross several TCP segments.
texts.text: In your Lab 0 VM, from your repository root, using your own server and client. Pick a port (5000 below) and keep it throughout. Use a test file of random bytes between 200 and 400 KiB. Loopback carries segments of up to about 64 KB, so a file that size makes the GET response cross several TCP segments.

texts.label: code
texts.orig: mkdir -p server-files evidence scratch # scratch/ is never committed head -c 262144 /dev/urandom > scratch/photo.bin # 256 KiB of synthetic data # Terminal 1: the server ./etp-server --port 5000 --root server-files # Terminal 2: start the capture (either line; sudo if permission is denied) tshark -i lo -s 200 -f "tcp port 5000" -w evidence/pa1-capture.pcap tcpdump -i lo -s 200 -Z $USER -w evidence/pa1-capture.pcap tcp port 5000 # Terminal 3: one PUT session, then one GET session, then ss within a minute C="./etp-client --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5000 --name YOURNAME" $C put scratch/photo.bin photo.bin $C get photo.bin scratch/copy.bin cmp scratch/photo.bin scratch/copy.bin && echo identical ss -tan state time-wait '( sport = :5000 or dport = :5000 )' \ > evidence/time-wait.txt # Terminal 2: stop the capture with Ctrl-C
texts.text: mkdir -p server-files evidence scratch # scratch/ is never committed head -c 262144 /dev/urandom > scratch/photo.bin # 256 KiB of synthetic data # Terminal 1: the server ./etp-server --port 5000 --root server-files # Terminal 2: start the capture (either line; sudo if permission is denied) tshark -i lo -s 200 -f "tcp port 5000" -w evidence/pa1-capture.pcap tcpdump -i lo -s 200 -Z $USER -w evidence/pa1-capture.pcap tcp port 5000 # Terminal 3: one PUT session, then one GET session, then ss within a minute C="./etp-client --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5000 --name YOURNAME" $C put scratch/photo.bin photo.bin $C get photo.bin scratch/copy.bin cmp scratch/photo.bin scratch/copy.bin && echo identical ss -tan state time-wait '( sport = :5000 or dport = :5000 )' \ > evidence/time-wait.txt # Terminal 2: stop the capture with Ctrl-C

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The facts block - eight values about your GET session, read from your capture, in the etp-facts block. The grader computes the same values from your capture and compares. Each value that matches earns a point. The two server-to-client counts cover all three of the server's responses in that session (HELLO_OK, GET_OK and BYE_OK), each frame counted once, as captured.

texts.orig: Five questions - answered in your own words, each in a paragraph or two, using your own numbers. In brief:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Q1 The handshake. The three segments, their flags and raw numbers; why the third segment's acknowledgment number is what it is; the MSS and what sets it.
texts.text: Q1 The handshake. The three segments, their flags and raw numbers; why the third segment's acknowledgment number is what it is; the MSS and what sets it.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Q2 Your protocol on the wire. The GET request's header and the GET_OK header, decoded field by field from the hex; the arithmetic that adds up the server's payload bytes.
texts.text: Q2 Your protocol on the wire. The GET request's header and the GET_OK header, decoded field by field from the hex; the arithmetic that adds up the server's payload bytes.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Q3 Byte stream, not messages. How many segments carried the GET_OK response, their sizes, whether messages and segments line up, and where your code deals with that.
texts.text: Q3 Byte stream, not messages. How many segments carried the GET_OK response, their sizes, whether messages and segments line up, and where your code deals with that.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Q4 Teardown and TIME-WAIT. Who closed first and why; which end is in TIME-WAIT, for how long, and why that is the reason for SO_REUSEADDR.
texts.text: Q4 Teardown and TIME-WAIT. Who closed first and why; which end is in TIME-WAIT, for how long, and why that is the reason for SO_REUSEADDR.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Q5 What an observer learns. What someone holding this capture knows about your session, what the 200-byte snap length hides and does not, and what kind of protection would change that.

texts.orig: You may use generative AI tools in this project. Working engineers do, and learning to use them well is part of what this course should teach you. But the point of these assignments is that you learn network programming: how a byte stream behaves, how framing works, how a server survives its clients, how reliability is built from loss. A tool that does that thinking for you takes the learning with it, and the final exam, the project, and your first job will find the gap.
